siding_exposure_m.note: INVENTED WITHIN A STOCK SET, NOT DERIVED. No source states the exposed face of any Chicago building's siding. The value is one of four period mill sidings — 4.5, 5, 5.5 or 6 in to the weather; this roof wears 5.5 in — dealt in this building's own parcel recipe: drawn on this record's stable key from the stocks its household class may hang (5 in, 5.5 in or 6 in; T-1839, docs/LIBERTIES.md L352), then advanced within them so that no roof of the parcel standing within 60 m hangs the same course. It is NOT keyed to a construction season the way the named buildings' stocks are: this record's 1835-01-01 is the programme's count-unit convention and not a date anything was built, so keying to it would deal every anonymous roof in the town one stock. The separation is the surface variety T-0049 reconstructs, not a claim about 1835. docs/LIBERTIES.md L148 owns the invention and the recipe half is recorded beside it, under `tools/siding_stock.py`.

land_owner.value: The ground was entered by Robert A Kenzie, 7 May 1831
land_owner.note: KINZIE'S ADDITION. The north fraction of section 10 is the section north of the river, which is why the register prints 102.29 acres and not a quarter's 160. It is resolved as the section's own grid box clipped to the committed north bank of the main stem (`e1834_harbor_cut/shoreline.geojson`), so no boundary here is authored. The two rows the register carries for it — one plain, one with the school-section marker — are the same entry printed twice. THE REGISTER SPELLS THE PURCHASER MORE THAN ONE WAY for this same tract — Robert A Kenzie; Robert A Kinzie — and the spellings are carried rather than merged, which is the land_sales crosswalk's standing rule: tract agreement is where two spellings MIGHT be one man and is never proof that they are. THE ROOF IS AN INVENTION AND THIS CANNOT OUTRANK IT. The footprint stands 28 m inside the tract's nearest boundary, which on a documented building would carry the middle tier, but this building was dealt to its lot by a recipe and is not there. The tract is real and the register's words about it are read; what is graded here is the claim that THIS roof stands on it, and that claim is the recipe's. WHAT THIS ROW CLAIMS AND WHAT IT DOES NOT. It claims that the tract the Illinois State Archives' land-sale register describes contains this structure's committed position — the patent for this ground was ENTERED by this man on this date. It does not claim he still held the ground on 1 July 1835, that he lived here, or that he ever stood on it: a sale is a transaction, and the register's only column about residence names a county. THE SECTION LINES ARE CONSTRUCTED, NOT TRACED (L219): the grid is carried from the single PLSS corner at State & Madison, on the plat's own east-west bearing, in nominal one-mile squares.

persons.note: A CONTEMPORARY CHICAGO PAPER OF 1833-1835 PRINTS THIS PERSON BY NAME IN THE TOWN. Read from newspaper_1833_1835. persons.name: Thomas Hoit
persons.note: A DOCUMENTED PERSON, AND NO TRADE IS CLAIMED BECAUSE THE PAPERS GIVE NONE. The corpus prints 'Hoit, Thomas' and 'Mr. Thomas Hoit' and places them at Chicago; it does not say what they did for a living, where this household lived, who else was in it, or when it came. The occupation therefore reads `none_recorded`, this dataset's own word for an absent record, rather than a trade reasoned from the company they keep — the absence is the finding. Cited at the Democrat of 24 September 1834, column 2; the Democrat of 19 August 1835, column 20. THE CORPUS PRINTS THIS PERSON IN 2 SEPARATE ISSUES. A transient is printed once and is gone; recurrence across the run is the paper's own evidence that the town kept dealing with them. A place the corpus associates with a person is where the paper does business with them and not a statement about where they slept. No figure is drawn (docs/LIBERTIES.md L1). READ THROUGH A TRANSCRIPTION, not a scan: the owner's ruling of 2026-08-28 grades a transcription-mediated reading as documented, and the source record for the run states that standard and its limits. A scan read that confirms or corrects the name upgrades this entry.

residents.research_note: MINTED FROM THE NEWSPAPER REGISTER (T-0373) BY A RESIDENCY TEST, NOT BY A TRADE. T-0376's pass mints the register's `new_resident` people whose trade the papers print; this one takes the rest, where there is no trade to anchor anybody and a printed name on its own proves only that a Chicago paper set the type. The test asks the corpus two questions instead: does it place this person inside the town and NOWHERE outside it, and does a second independent witness corroborate a bare 'Chicago' — an address at street level, print in two or more issues, or print beside two or more people this reconstruction already holds. THE CORPUS PRINTS THIS PERSON IN 2 SEPARATE ISSUES. A transient is printed once and is gone; recurrence across the run is the paper's own evidence that the town kept dealing with them. The household around them is a CONTAINER and not an argument: one member, no dwelling, no division, no family, no recorded trade, and every one of those absences written as unattested rather than filled in from the shape of the rest of the town. That the person is a HOUSEHOLD is the one invention here and it is recorded as docs/LIBERTIES.md L213. tools/mint_placed_residents.py derives the whole minted set and prints every candidate it refused, with the reason.

persons.name: Edward Trimble
persons.note: PROJECTED RESIDENT. Documented in Chicago post-office evidence but not independently corroborated strongly enough for attested circa-1835 residence. KNOWN ONLY FROM THE POST OFFICE, IN ONE RETURN. The papers print 'Edward Trimble' in a single return of letters uncalled-for at the Chicago post office — the Democrat of 2 July 1834, column 33, reprinted over 3 consecutive issues — dated 1834-07-02 to 1834-07-16. Nothing else in the corpus names this person: no trade, no street, no household, no arrival, so every other claim here is written unattested in its own block. WHAT THAT IS WORTH: a correspondent believed a person of this name reachable at Chicago on that date, and nothing further — not that they lived here, kept a trade here, or were here on 1 July 1835. It is the weakest evidence this project accepts for a resident, and a source placing them elsewhere retires the record. THE ARGUMENT EVERY RECORD OF THIS KIND SHARES is written once instead of once per file: the ruling of 2026-08-30 and what it cost the town (docs/LIBERTIES.md L214), the refusals and the transcription standard behind the reading (tools/mint_letter_list_residents.py). No figure is drawn (L1).

residents.research_note: MINTED FROM THE LETTER LISTS (T-0378, T-0379). THE HOUSEHOLD IS A CONTAINER, NOT AN ARGUMENT: every other record here argues for a household, and this one argues for a PERSON. `data/residents/` cannot carry a person outside a household, so one was written around them and told to claim nothing — one member, no dwelling, no division, no trade, no family, no arrival beyond the paper's bound. tools/mint_letter_list_residents.py derives the set and prints every refusal, `--gate` proves no record here gained a roof, a trade or a second member, and docs/LIBERTIES.md L214 carries the change of scale.

what_it_supplies: A 665-roof production target with independently reconcilable group, district, level, and construction totals.

what_it_does_not_supply: A surviving July 1835 building census or parcel-by-parcel roof register.
Exact locations, dimensions, appearance, occupants, or construction dates for anonymous roofs.
Authority to replace stronger building-specific evidence already represented in the dataset.
